name: Symbolic Regression
analogy: Think of it as breeding formulas the way a farmer breeds crops. Hundreds of random recipes are tried, the ones that fit the data best are crossed with each other, and after many generations a short recipe you can read is left standing.

steps.title: Choose the building blocks
steps.description: You supply the pieces a formula may use: the input features, some constants, and operations such as add, multiply, divide and a squashing function. The model never goes outside this kit.
steps.inExample: The kit holds momentum, average true range and volume ratio as inputs, plus add, subtract, multiply, divide and the hyperbolic tangent.

steps.title: Create a random population of formulas
steps.description: Each formula is built as a tree of operations with features and constants at the leaves. The first generation is mostly nonsense, which is expected.
steps.inExample: A population of 2,000 random formulas is built, such as momentum times a constant, or volume ratio divided by average true range.

steps.title: Score every formula against the target
steps.description: Each formula is run on the training bars and its predictions are compared with what happened. A small penalty is added for length, so a short formula beats a long one with the same accuracy.
steps.inExample: Each formula predicts the 6-bar-ahead change in points; formulas with large errors or very long trees score poorly.

steps.title: Keep the better formulas
steps.description: Better-scoring formulas are more likely to be chosen as parents. Weak ones mostly disappear, which is what pushes the population toward formulas that fit.
steps.inExample: The best 200 of the 2,000 formulas get most of the parenting slots in the next generation.

steps.title: Cross and mutate
steps.description: Two parents swap randomly chosen branches to make a child that mixes both. Occasionally a branch, operation or constant is replaced at random to introduce something new.
steps.inExample: One parent's momentum branch is swapped with another parent's volatility denominator, and a constant of nine in a third is nudged to eleven.

steps.title: Repeat for many generations, then pick one
steps.description: Scoring, selection, crossing and mutation repeat. At the end you are left with a short list of formulas trading off accuracy against length, and you choose one by checking it on bars it was not evolved on.
steps.inExample: After 80 generations the chosen formula has ten building blocks: eleven times a squashed momentum term, divided by one plus a twentieth of average true range.

useFor.task: Finding a readable formula for a signal
useFor.example: Searching for a short expression that links momentum, volatility and volume features on 5-minute bars of Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures (MNQ) to the move over the next 30 minutes.

useFor.task: Replacing a black box with a formula
useFor.example: Fitting a formula to the predictions of a trained gradient boosting model so a simplified version can be inspected line by line.
Finding that a ratio of volume to volatility matters more than either alone, something a straight-line fit would never express.
Evolving a separate short formula for trending and ranging regimes and comparing what each one emphasises.

avoidWhen: You want the strongest predictive accuracy and do not need to read the result; gradient boosting or a neural network usually fits complex patterns better than a short formula.
The data is small or very noisy, because the search will happily evolve a formula that memorises noise; a simpler regularised model is safer.

example.scenario: Symbolic regression is run on a year of 5-minute Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures (MNQ) bars to find a formula for the price change over the next 6 bars, then applied to one new bar.

input.summary: The training table the search evolves against, and the feature values of the one new bar being scored.

fields.name: training bars
fields.meaning: How many five-minute bars the formulas were scored on.

fields.name: target
fields.value: price change over the next 6 bars, in points
fields.meaning: The quantity every formula tries to predict.

fields.name: population size
fields.meaning: How many candidate formulas exist in each generation.

fields.name: generations
fields.meaning: How many rounds of selection, crossing and mutation were run.

fields.name: momentum over 6 bars
fields.value: down about a third of a percent
fields.meaning: Feature value for the new bar, read in percent: price has fallen about a third of a percent over the last 30 minutes.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: Feature value for the new bar: the recent typical bar range.

output.summary: A short formula written in words, its size, its scores, and its prediction for the new bar.

fields.name: chosen formula
fields.value: eleven times the hyperbolic tangent of momentum in percent, divided by one plus one twentieth of average true range
fields.meaning: The readable expression the search settled on; it gives a forecast in points.

fields.name: formula size
fields.meaning: The count of operations, features and constants in the formula tree.

fields.name: average error on training bars
fields.meaning: How far off the formula is on average on the bars it was evolved on.

fields.name: average error on later bars
fields.meaning: The same error on held-back bars, which shows whether the formula holds up.

fields.name: prediction for the new bar
fields.meaning: The formula's forecast of the price change over the next 6 bars, about 4 US dollars per contract against a long position.

example.reading: A prediction of about 2 points against a 22-point typical bar range is a faint lean, not a signal. The value of the result is the formula itself: read which features it uses and whether the shape makes market sense, then test it on later walk-forward folds with costs before trusting it.
